title: Rome: works condignly merit second justification; Reformed deny 'merit' vs grace
source_text: LVIII. Sed praeterea Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, alio sensu opera justificare docent; quia, scilicet, juxta mentem illorum, merentur ex condigno secundam, quam vocant, justificationem, id est, augmentum gratiae illius, per quam homo in sanctitate & justitia crescit; quae est unanimis eorum sententia. Verum admittimus quidem exercitio bonorum operum hominem in justitia & sanctitate proficere, & majorem a Christo, secundum illius promissa, gratiam obtinere. Sed tamen negamus propterea dicendum esse, quod opera nostra gratiam istam mereantur. Quoniam, videlicet, inter se pugnant gratia, & debitum. Nec gratia est, id est, donum Dei gratuitum, quod operibus nostris ex justitia debetur. Siquidem Apostolus diserte opponit illud quod est secundum gratiam, ei quod est secundum debitum. Rom. 4. v. 4. Quo pertinet illud ejusdem Apostoli, Si ex gratia, jam non ex operibus; alioquin gratia jam non est gratia: si autem ex operibus, jam non ex gratia; alioquin opus jam non est opus. Rom. 11. v. 6. Sed quaestionis hujusce momentum accuratius alias, Deo favente, expendemus, quum de Meritis operum ex professo agemus.
pass_a_gloss: But further the Doctors of the Roman Church teach that works justify in another sense: because, namely, according to their mind, they merit from condignity the second justification, as they call it—that is, an increase of that grace by which a man grows in holiness and righteousness; which is their unanimous opinion. Truly we do indeed admit that by the exercise of good works a man advances in righteousness and holiness, and obtains greater grace from Christ according to his promises. But nevertheless we deny that it is therefore to be said that our works merit that grace. Because, namely, grace and debt fight against each other. Nor is that grace—that is, a free gift of God—which is owed from justice to our works. Since the Apostle expressly opposes that which is according to grace to that which is according to debt (Rom 4:4). To which pertains that of the same Apostle: If by grace, then no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace: but if from works, then no longer from grace; otherwise work is no longer work (Rom 11:6). But the moment of this question we will weigh more accurately elsewhere, God favoring, when we treat of the Merits of works ex professo.
pass_b_english: Rome unanimously: works condignly merit 'second justification' (growth in grace).
Reformed admit growth by good works under Christ's promise, but deny 'merit'—grace and debt conflict (Rom 4; 11).
